extracted.intended_audience: employers, HR professionals, labor and employment attorneys, and policymakers/regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards from the FTC final rule on non-compete clauses, describing definitions (e.g., senior executive, common enterprise), prohibited practices, justifications, and acceptable alternatives for employers and legal advisors to follow for compliance and rule interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-making authority / position excludes subsidiary-only authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission added language to the definitions of “policy-making authority” and “policy-making position” to exclude from the definition of “senior executives” workers with policy-making authority over only a subsidiary or affiliate of a common enterprise who do not have policy-making authority over the common enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A worker must have policy-making authority with respect to the common enterprise as a whole, not just a segment, to be a senior executive. Department heads and other highly paid non-senior executives who only control a component are unlikely to meet the job duties test and lack sufficient bargaining power to avoid exploitation and coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job duties test identifies workers with highest authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The job duties test identifies the workers with the highest levels of authority in an organization, i.e., the workers most likely to have bargaining power and a bespoke, negotiated agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on real-world implications and authority rather than formal titles; even workers with senior executive titles may fail the job duties test if their duties do not reflect enterprise-wide authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common enterprise looks beyond legal entities (integrated business entities)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered a “common enterprise” the Commission looks beyond legal corporate entities to whether there is a common enterprise of “integrated business entities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics indicating a common enterprise include: maintaining officers, directors, and workers in common; operating under common control; sharing offices; commingling funds; and sharing advertising and marketing. This analysis informs whether subsidiary executives are excluded from 'senior executive' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from policy-making definitions applies only to common enterprises
rubrics_metrics.description: This exclusion from the definitions of “policy-making authority” and “policy-making position” applies only to common enterprises; for subsidiaries or affiliates that are not part of a common enterprise, a worker could qualify as a senior executive if they have policy-making authority over that subsidiary or affiliate and meet all of the requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine common enterprise status first; if no common enterprise exists, an affiliate's head may qualify as senior executive for purposes of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use defined terms 'business entity' and 'natural person' for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission substituted “business entity” (instead of SEC's “registrant” or 17 CFR’s “organization”) and “natural person” (instead of “person”) in relevant definitions to align with §910.1 and the scope of this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting and interpretation should use the rule's defined terms consistently rather than SEC-specific terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt FLSA exemptions for senior executive exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission does not adopt the FLSA exemptions for purposes of this final rule because it would exempt millions of non-competes that harm competition and workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although commenters urged use of FLSA categories (executive, administrative, professional) and DOL salary thresholds, the Commission prefers brighter-line rules tailored to non-compete concerns and views FLSA salary methodology only as a useful benchmark for highly compensated employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret / confidential information exceptions are not adopted
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is not adopting exceptions based on access to trade secrets or other intellectual property for allowing non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite commenter requests to exempt workers with access to trade secrets (including highly paid/skilled workers), the Commission explains in Parts V.D.1 and V.D.2 why such exceptions are inappropriate and unnecessary given alternative protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid definitions based only on job titles or rigid lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions based on job titles alone would be inadequate because employers define job titles differently, and a title might not accurately reflect a worker's job duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title-based or fixed-number approaches (e.g., SEC Reg S-K approach) can be misaligned across firms of different sizes and would produce unequal application; prefer duties-based analysis combined with compensation threshold to balance administrability and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test: job duties plus compensation threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission pairs a relatively easy-to-apply job duties test with a compensation threshold to maximize administrability and clarity while identifying those senior executives most likely to have bargained for non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-part design aims to limit fact-intensive litigation and in terrorem effects while capturing workers who plausibly negotiated bespoke agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of business exception covers partners/shareholders in many cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals to except partners, shareholders, and similar groups are likely covered by the sale of business exception if they sell their share of the business upon leaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applicability of the sale of business exception before crafting separate exemptions for owners or equity-holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited practices for senior executives (§910.2(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person: (i) to enter into or attempt to enter into a non-compete clause; (ii) to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause entered into after the effective date; or (iii) to represent that the senior executive is subject to a non-compete clause, where the non-compete clause was entered into after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §910.2(a)(2) differs from §910.2(a)(1) only in that enforcement and representation prohibitions apply only to non-competes entered into after the effective date; existing pre-effective-date non-competes with senior executives are not prohibited. The good-faith exception in §910.3 applies to these prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing non-competes with senior executives are not prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has determined not to prohibit existing non-competes with senior executives—i.e., non-competes entered into before the effective date—from remaining in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-effective-date restrictions (enforcement/representation) apply only to agreements entered after the effective date; enforcement of pre-existing non-competes remains governed by other rule provisions and the good-faith exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed justifications must be legally cognizable, non-pretextual, and narrowly tailored
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendants raise justifications as an affirmative defense, they must be legally cognizable, and non-pretextual, and any restriction used to bring about the benefit must be narrowly tailored to limit any adverse impact on competitive conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pecuniary benefit to the actor is not cognizable as a justification; courts sometimes decline to consider justifications at all. Burdensome restrictions require narrow tailoring and demonstration that less-restrictive alternatives are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed business justifications do not overcome rule's finding
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed business justifications for non-competes (e.g., to increase investment in human capital, client retention, trade secret protection) do not alter the Commission's determination that non-competes are an unfair method of competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission finds alternatives exist that burden competition to a lesser degree and that asserted benefits do not justify the considerable harms from non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evidence must be weighed critically (methodology and causal inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission evaluates empirical studies critically, giving more weight to studies measuring changes in enforceability (rather than use) and to studies distinguishing relevant outcomes (e.g., core vs advanced training).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Starr study has limits (uses non-compete use, doesn't distinguish core vs advanced training); Jeffers, Johnson/Lipsitz, Shi get varying weights depending on measurement of enforceability, sample, and outcome. Use of correlational comparisons (use vs non-use) receives minimal weight for causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers have less-restrictive alternatives to non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers have alternatives to non-competes for protecting valuable investments that burden competition to a less significant degree, such as trade secret law, NDAs, fixed-duration employment contracts, and competing for labor via pay/conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternatives are more narrowly tailored and preserve worker mobility. The Commission cites experience in California, North Dakota, and Oklahoma showing industries that rely on trade secrets and skilled labor can thrive without enforceable non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secret law as viable alternative (UTSA, DTSA, EEA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade secret law (UTSA, DTSA) provides employers with well-established protections, including injunctive and monetary relief; the EEA makes trade secret theft a federal crime with criminal fines and forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secret law burdens competition less than non-competes because it targets misuse/disclosure rather than barring employment; DTSA allows civil ex parte seizures in extraordinary circumstances. High volumes of trade secret litigation indicate firms view trade secret law as viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: NDAs are a viable alternative when appropriately tailored
rubrics_metrics.description: NDAs (confidentiality agreements) are contracts preventing disclosure/use of confidential information; appropriately tailored NDAs burden competition less than non-competes because they generally do not prevent workers from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule prohibits only NDAs that are so overbroad as to function to prevent a worker from seeking or accepting employment or operating a business. Most states enforce NDAs more readily than non-competes; high co-occurrence exists between non-competes and NDAs, so tailoring matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other statutory and contractual protections (patents, invention assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional means for protecting investments include patent law and invention assignment agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should consider intellectual property regimes and assignment agreements before resorting to non-competes that unduly restrict competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fact-intensive definitions that create in terrorem effects for low-wage workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions or exemptions that require more fact-intensive analysis (e.g., golden parachute analogues, detailed duties inquiries) would require market participants to conduct analyses for more workers and are likely to have in terrorem effects for lower-wage workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer administrable, brighter-line approaches to limit litigation costs and chilling effects on worker mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith exception applies (§910.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good-faith exception in §910.3 is applicable to the relevant prohibitions with respect to senior executives and is explained elsewhere in the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties asserting or subject to enforcement should evaluate applicability of the good-faith exception under §910.3 when analyzing conduct under §910.2.
